newsitem.title: USA: High Court won't review Denver bond ruling appeal.
newsitem.headline: High Court won't review Denver bond ruling appeal.

text.p: The U.S. Supreme Court on Monday refused to review an appeals court finding that the city of Denver says gives bondholders an unlawful green light to sue cities for damages under the federal securities laws.

The High Court's decision not to consider the November 1996 ruling by the 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals means that the two-year-old class-action lawsuit involving $3 billion of tax-exempt bonds issued to construct the $5 billion Denver International Airport can proceed unhindered.

The original lawsuit filed by Bonnie Sonnenfeld and other investors charged that Denver knew, but failed to disclose, problems with a state-of-the-art baggage handling system that triggered an 18-month delay in the airport's opening and a downgrade of the bonds' ratings.
But Denver moved to dismiss the case, saying that there is no implied private cause of action against municipalities under the antifraud provisions of the federal securities laws.

Denver said that while amendments to the securities laws passed by Congress in 1975 make clear that the SEC can sue municipalities for securities fraud violations, the 1975 language does not explicitly say private entities can sue.
The appeals panel rejected the argument in an 11-page ruling on November 12, and Denver turned to the High Court for review of the issue.

The city argued in a recent brief that the appeals' decision "is bad policy as well as bad law." It warned that giving investors a private right of action against municipal issuers "will have serious adverse effects on the ability of municipalities to use bonds to fund their capital needs."

But bondholders said in an April response that subjecting municipalities to private liability furthers "the fundamental purposes of the federal securities laws - protecting the investing public, promoting public confidence in our capital markets, and deterring wrongdoing."

Bondholders rejected a statement by Denver that the appeals court ruling is the first time a court has exposed a municipality to a private action. They pointed to legal action resulting from a massive default of Washington Public Power Supply System bonds in the 1980s.
The bondholders' case is against both the city and county of Denver and bond industry professionals.
Discovery in the case has been proceeding despite the appeal.
